tunnel.usageNote: A common word. Good to learn.
tunnel.example: The train went through a long tunnel.
tunnel.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

tusk.meaning: One of the two very long teeth that grow out of the mouth of an elephant or mammoth.
tusk.usageNote: A common word. Good to understand.
tusk.example: Elephants are killed for their tusks.
tusk.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

uncover.meaning: To take a cover off; here, to take a finger off a hole.
uncover.usageNote: A common word. Good to understand.
uncover.example: She uncovered the pot to look at the soup.

untie.meaning: To open a knot in a rope or string.
untie.usageNote: A common word. Good to understand.

vanish.meaning: To go away suddenly so you cannot see it any more; to disappear.
vanish.usageNote: A common word. Good to learn.
vanish.example: The sun vanished behind a cloud.

wail.meaning: To cry or shout in a long, high, sad voice.
wail.usageNote: A common word. Good to understand.

warn.meaning: To tell someone that something bad or dangerous may happen.
warn.usageNote: A common word. Good to understand.
warn.example: Mom warned us not to swim in the river.

waved.meaning: Moved her long nose in a happy way.
waved.whyHard: This word is less common than the school words for the same idea.

waving.meaning: Moving a hand as a greeting.
waving.whyHard: This word is less common than the school words for the same idea.

whew.meaning: A sound you make when you are glad that something bad is over.
whew.usageNote: A common word. Good to understand.
whew.example: Whew! We caught the bus just in time.
whew.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

whisper.usageNote: A common word. Good to learn.
whisper.example: She whispered the answer to her friend.

whoa.meaning: A word you say when you are surprised, or to tell a horse to stop.
whoa.usageNote: A common word. Good to understand.
whoa.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

wick.meaning: The string in a candle or lamp that you light.
wick.usageNote: You only need to understand it for this book.
wick.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

wildly.meaning: In a fast, wild way that is hard to control.
wildly.usageNote: A common word. Good to understand.
wildly.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

windswept.usageNote: You only need to understand it for this book.
windswept.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

wipe.meaning: To clean something by moving a cloth or your hand over it.
wipe.usageNote: A common word. Good to learn.
wipe.example: Please wipe the table after dinner.
wipe.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

wooden.usageNote: A common word. Good to understand.
wooden.example: We sat at a big wooden table.
wooden.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

woolly.meaning: Covered with long, thick hair, like wool.
woolly.usageNote: Mostly used for the Ice Age animals "woolly mammoth" and "woolly rhino". Also spelled "wooly".
woolly.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

wrap.meaning: To put cloth or paper all the way around something.
wrap.usageNote: A common word. Good to learn.
wrap.example: She wrapped the present in red paper.

yell.usageNote: A common word. Good to learn.
yell.example: Don't yell at your little brother.

yikes.meaning: A word you say when you are suddenly afraid or surprised.
yikes.usageNote: Informal. Used a lot by children and in stories.
yikes.example: Yikes! There's a spider on my arm!
yikes.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

yowl.meaning: A long loud cry, like the cry of an angry cat.
yowl.usageNote: You only need to understand it for this book.
yowl.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

about to.meaning: Going to do something very soon.
about to.example: about to set out in search of the third thing
about to.usageNote: Very common. "I was about to call you" means "I was going to call you right then".

as soon as possible.example: Don’t you want to save Morgan as soon as possible
as soon as possible.usageNote: Very common. Often written "ASAP" in messages.

at a distance.example: moved along with them, at a distance
at a distance.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

at least.meaning: Used to say that a situation is a little good, even if the rest is bad.
at least.example: But at least the wind wasn’t blowing
at least.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

bathing suit.example: change out of my bathing suit
bathing suit.usageNote: A little old-fashioned. Today people often say "swimsuit".

be right back.meaning: I will come back very soon.
be right back.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

cave bear.meaning: A very big kind of bear that lived in caves in the Ice Age. It is now extinct (all dead).
cave bear.example: The great cave bears of the Ice Age
cave bear.usageNote: You only need to understand it for this book.

caved in.meaning: When the ground or a roof caves in, it suddenly falls down into a hole.
caved in.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

change out of.meaning: To take off some clothes and put on other clothes.
change out of.example: change out of my bathing suit
change out of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

come into view.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

come out.meaning: When the sun comes out, it appears from behind the clouds.
come out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

cro magnon.meaning: The name for early modern humans who lived in Europe in the Ice Age, about 45,000 to 10,000 years ago.
cro magnon.example: Early modern humans were called Cro-Magnons
cro magnon.usageNote: Say it "kroh-MAN-yon". Scientists today often say "early modern humans" instead.

flip through.meaning: To turn the pages of a book quickly.
flip through.example: flipped through the Ice Age book
flip through.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

freeze to death.meaning: To die because you are too cold. People also say it when they are just very cold.
freeze to death.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get in a panic.meaning: To become very afraid and stop thinking clearly.
get in a panic.example: We just got in a panic
get in a panic.usageNote: People also say "panic" or "get into a panic".

give up on.meaning: To stop hoping for something or stop trying to do it.
give up on.example: He gave up on the idea
give up on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

good thinking.meaning: A friendly way to say "That is a clever idea".
good thinking.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

head back.example: We’d better head back to the tree house
head back.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

hold on.meaning: To hold something firmly so you do not fall or let go.
hold on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

hollow out.meaning: To make an empty space inside something.
hollow out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

ice age.meaning: A very long time in the past when ice covered large parts of the earth. The last Ice Age ended about 12,000 years ago.
ice age.usageNote: Usually written with capital letters: the Ice Age.

in search of.example: set out in search of the third thing
in search of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in the distance.example: the tall, bare trees in the distance
in the distance.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

keep from.meaning: To stop yourself doing something. "To keep from falling off" means so that she would not fall off.
keep from.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

keep it up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

let out.meaning: To make a sound, like a cry or a shout.
let out.example: the mammoth let out a cry
let out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

no sign of.meaning: You cannot see or find it anywhere.
no sign of.example: There was no sign of the Pennsylvania book
no sign of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

no wonder.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

oh brother.meaning: What you say when you are tired of something or a bit annoyed. It is not about a real brother.
oh brother.usageNote: Informal and a little old-fashioned, but still used.

oh man.meaning: What you say when you are surprised, worried or excited.
oh man.example: Oh man,” he said. “Where is he

out of sight.meaning: In a place where you cannot see it.
out of sight.example: Then they moved out of sight
out of sight.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

pick up speed.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

rope ladder.example: She was climbing the rope ladder up to the tree house
rope ladder.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

run out of.meaning: To have no more of something.
run out of.example: until he ran out of breath
run out of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

set out.example: about to set out in search of the third thing
set out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

ta da.meaning: What you say when you show someone something surprising, like a magic trick.
ta da.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

under a spell.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

wait a second.meaning: Stop for a moment; wait a short time.
wait a second.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

watch out for.meaning: To be careful of something dangerous.
watch out for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

woolly mammoth.meaning: A kind of mammoth with long thick hair that lived in cold places in the Ice Age.
woolly mammoth.example: Annie was sitting on a woolly mammoth
woolly mammoth.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

woolly rhino.meaning: A kind of rhino with long thick hair that lived in the Ice Age.
woolly rhino.example: Then a woolly rhino joined them
woolly rhino.usageNote: You only need to understand it for this book.

paragraphs.context: One summer day in Frog Creek, Pennsylvania, a mysterious tree house appeared
paragraphs.mainIdea: A magic tree house appears in the woods of a small town.
paragraphs.simple: One summer day, a strange tree house suddenly appeared in the woods of Frog Creek, Pennsylvania.

background.note: Frog Creek is a made-up small town. Pennsylvania is a real state in the east of the United States.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie visited dinosaurs, knights, an Egyptian queen
paragraphs.mainIdea: This tells us about Jack and Annie's first six trips.
paragraphs.simple: Before this book, the tree house took Jack and Annie to the time of the dinosaurs, to knights and castles, to ancient Egypt, to pirates, to ninjas in old Japan, and to the Amazon rain forest. Each trip is a different book in the series.

background.note: A queen of ancient Egypt, more than 3,000 years ago. The Egyptians built the pyramids.
A very big, hot, wet forest in South America, around the Amazon River.

paragraphs.context: Along the way, they discovered that the tree house belonged to Morgan le Fay
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree house belongs to Morgan le Fay, a magic librarian.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie learned that the tree house is Morgan le Fay's. She can do magic, and she travels to different times and places to collect books for King Arthur.

background.note: A woman who can do magic in the old British stories about King Arthur. In this series she is kind and loves books.
A king in old British stories. He and his knights lived in a castle called Camelot. Nobody knows if he was a real person.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie also found a note from Morgan
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan is in trouble, and Jack and Annie must find four special things to help her.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie found a note from Morgan. Someone has put magic on her, and she is not free. To help her, Jack and Annie must find four special things.

paragraphs.context: Now Jack and Annie and Peanut are about to set out
paragraphs.mainIdea: Now the children and their mouse are going to look for the third special thing.
paragraphs.simple: Jack, Annie and Peanut the mouse are ready to start a new trip. They will look for the third special thing in this book, Sunset of the Sabertooth.
paragraphs.tone: The three dots (…) make you wait a moment, like a little drum roll, before the name of the book.

paragraphs.context: She and Jack were passing the Frog Creek woods
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack and Annie are walking home from a swimming class.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie were walking past the Frog Creek woods. They were going home after their swimming class.

background.note: Short for the YMCA, a sports and community centre found in many American towns. Many children have swimming classes there.

paragraphs.context: Jack sighed. He gave up on the idea
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack forgets about changing his clothes and follows Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Jack let out a long breath. He stopped thinking about changing out of his swimming clothes.
paragraphs.tone: Jack is a little annoyed, but he always goes with his sister in the end.

paragraphs.context: On the M were a moonstone and a mango
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children look at the things they found on their last two trips.
paragraphs.simple: A moonstone and a mango were lying on the big letter M. These were the special things Jack and Annie found on their last two trips.

background.note: A white, shining stone. Jack and Annie found it on their trip to old Japan (book 5).
A tropical fruit. They found it in the Amazon rain forest (book 6).

paragraphs.context: The grove was on a wide, white plain
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree house is in a group of trees on a large, flat, snowy land.
paragraphs.simple: The trees stood on a big, flat, white piece of land. Far away there were tall walls of rock.

paragraphs.context: I’m c-cold,” said Annie. Her teeth chattered
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie is very cold.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says she is cold. Her teeth hit each other because of the cold, and she pulls her towel around her.
paragraphs.tone: "C-cold" shows that Annie's teeth are chattering, so she cannot say the word smoothly. Later the book does the same with "Sq-squeak" and "f-freezing".

paragraphs.context: Ice Age?” said Annie. “No wonder we’re cold
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie understands why it is so cold.
paragraphs.simple: Annie hears the words "Ice Age". She says it is not surprising that they feel cold.
paragraphs.tone: A small joke: of course it is cold in a time called the "Ice Age".

background.note: A time long ago when the earth was much colder and ice covered large parts of it. The last Ice Age ended about 12,000 years ago.

paragraphs.context: Early modern humans were called Cro-Magnons
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book tells Jack about the Cro-Magnon people.
paragraphs.simple: The first modern people in Europe are called Cro-Magnons. At the end of the Ice Age, some of them lived in caves under cliffs.

background.note: The name comes from a cave in France called Cro-Magnon, where people found their bones in 1868. They looked like people today.

paragraphs.context: The Cro-Magnon family often hunted together
paragraphs.mainIdea: This tells us how Cro-Magnon families hunted big animals.
paragraphs.simple: Cro-Magnon families hunted together. They dug deep holes and covered them with branches. Then they chased reindeer and mammoths so that the animals fell into the holes.

paragraphs.context: No, it’s not,” said Jack. “They couldn’t live without hunting
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack says the Cro-Magnons had to hunt to stay alive.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says hunting is not bad for them. They needed food, and they had no shops to buy it.
paragraphs.tone: Jack talks like a teacher. "They didn't have supermarkets, you know" is a little funny, because of course people in the Ice Age had no supermarkets. The book comes back to this joke at the very end.

paragraphs.context: Forget it,” said Jack. “They don’t have books that tell them about us
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is afraid the cave people will think they are enemies.
paragraphs.simple: Jack tells Annie not to try to meet them. The Cro-Magnons know nothing about the children, so they may think the children want to hurt them and throw their spears.

paragraphs.context: Good thinking,” said Jack. “Now cover your head with your towel
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack likes Annie's idea and tells her to cover her head too.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says Annie's idea is clever. He tells her to put her towel over her head, because the body loses a lot of heat through the head.

paragraphs.context: The great cave bears of the Ice Age were over eight feet tall
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book says the cave belongs to a huge, dangerous cave bear.
paragraphs.simple: Cave bears in the Ice Age were more than two and a half meters tall. They were bigger and more dangerous than the bears of today. Their caves were full of the bones of older bears.

background.note: Americans use feet to measure. One foot is about 30 centimeters, so eight feet is about 2.4 meters.
Grizzly bears: large brown bears that live in North America today.

paragraphs.context: A booming snore shattered the air
paragraphs.mainIdea: The bear makes a very loud noise in its sleep.
paragraphs.simple: The bear snored very loudly, and the quiet cave was suddenly full of noise.

paragraphs.context: He probably never even woke up. We just got in a panic
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack thinks the bear did not wake up, and they were just afraid.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says the bear probably kept sleeping. They ran away only because they were very afraid.

paragraphs.context: Under a cliff was a wide ledge
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children see another cave, and this one looks warm.
paragraphs.simple: There was a wide shelf of rock under a cliff, and under it there was another cave. Light was coming out of this cave. It looked warm and safe.

paragraphs.context: Near the fire were knives, axes, and hollowed-out stones
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children see the tools of the cave people.
paragraphs.simple: There were stone knives, axes and stones with holes in them next to the fire.

paragraphs.context: Cro-Magnons made many things from animals, plants, and stone
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book tells how the Cro-Magnons made tools, music and ropes.
paragraphs.simple: The Cro-Magnons used animals, plants and stones to make things. They made flutes from mammoth bones. They twisted plant threads together to make ropes. They made axes and knives from stone.

background.note: People have found very old flutes made of bird and mammoth bones. Some are more than 40,000 years old, so they are some of the oldest musical instruments in the world.

paragraphs.context: From that pile of furry skins
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie found the coat in a pile of animal skins.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says she got the coat from a pile of soft animal skins. She thinks these are the cave people's clothes, and maybe someone is fixing them.

paragraphs.context: Cro-Magnons scraped reindeer skins with flint rocks
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book tells how the Cro-Magnons made clothes.
paragraphs.simple: The Cro-Magnons used sharp stones to clean reindeer skins and make them soft. Then they used needles made of bone to join the skins and make clothes.

background.note: People have found needles made of bone from more than 20,000 years ago. They even had a small hole for the thread, like needles today.

paragraphs.context: Cro-Magnons made stone lamps
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book tells how the Cro-Magnons made light.
paragraphs.simple: The Cro-Magnons made a hole in a stone and put animal fat in it. Then they used a piece of moss as a string and lit it, like a candle.

paragraphs.context: Too late—she had squeezed into the opening and was gone
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie goes into the tunnel before Jack can stop her.
paragraphs.simple: Jack was too slow. Annie had already pushed herself into the small hole and she was gone.

paragraphs.context: Crouching clown, he hurried toward her
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack goes through the tunnel and finds a very big cave.
paragraphs.simple: Jack bent down low and hurried to Annie. At the end of the small tunnel there was a huge cave with a high top.
paragraphs.tone: Note: "clown" is a printing mistake in this book. It should be "down": "Crouching down".

paragraphs.context: There were cave bears and lions, elk and reindeer
paragraphs.mainIdea: The paintings show many Ice Age animals.
paragraphs.simple: The pictures on the wall showed many animals: cave bears, lions, big deer, reindeer, wild cows, woolly rhinos and mammoths.

background.note: A big wild animal like a cow. Bison still live in North America and Europe today.
Rhinos with long thick hair that lived in the Ice Age. They are now extinct.

paragraphs.context: Maybe it’s an art gallery
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie thinks the painted cave is a place to look at art.
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks the cave may be a place where people go to look at pictures.
paragraphs.tone: Annie's idea is a little funny, because an art gallery is a modern place in a city.

paragraphs.context: These Ice Age beasts were painted 25,000 years ago
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book explains the cave paintings.
paragraphs.simple: People painted these animals 25,000 years ago. They painted animals that they hunted. Maybe they believed the pictures gave them power over the animals, so the hunt would go well.

background.note: Real Ice Age cave paintings can still be seen today, for example in the caves of Lascaux in France and Altamira in Spain. Many are about 17,000 to 36,000 years old.

paragraphs.context: Cave men may have been led by a sorcerer
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book tells about a magic leader of the cave people.
paragraphs.simple: Maybe the cave people had a leader who could do magic. People call him the "Master of the Animals". Maybe he wore reindeer horns to run fast like a reindeer, and an owl mask to see well like an owl.

background.note: A real cave painting in France, in the Trois-Frères cave, shows a figure that is part man and part animal, with antlers. People call it "The Sorcerer". Nobody knows for sure what it means.

paragraphs.context: Oh no!” cried Annie. “She must have crawled out
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie thinks Peanut left the bag while they looked at the pictures.
paragraphs.simple: Annie is worried. She thinks Peanut moved out of the backpack while they were looking at the paintings.

paragraphs.context: The wind blew harder. Snow swirled over the ground
paragraphs.mainIdea: The wind covers Peanut's footprints with snow.
paragraphs.simple: The wind got stronger. Snow moved round and round over the ground and covered the mouse's small footprints.

paragraphs.context: Jack followed her gaze. On one of the cliffs was a tiger
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack sees a huge tiger with long teeth on a cliff.
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked where Annie was looking. There was a very big tiger on a cliff. It had two long, sharp teeth.

background.term: A giant tiger with two long, sharp fangs
background.note: This is a sabertooth, sometimes called a "saber-toothed tiger". It was not really a tiger, but a big wild cat. Its front teeth could be more than 20 centimeters long.

paragraphs.context: The ground caved in, and Jack went with it
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ground suddenly falls in, and Jack falls into a hole.
paragraphs.simple: Suddenly the ground under Jack broke and fell down, and Jack fell down with it.

paragraphs.context: This is a trap,” Jack said
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack understands that they fell into a hunting trap.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says this hole is a trap. The cave people covered it with branches, and then snow covered the branches. So the children could not see the hole.

paragraphs.context: She was right. They were helpless
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children cannot get out of the deep hole.
paragraphs.simple: Annie was right. They could not do anything. The hole was too deep to climb out.

paragraphs.context: The sabertooth was the fiercest beast of the Ice Age
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book says the sabertooth was very dangerous.
paragraphs.simple: The sabertooth was the most dangerous animal of the Ice Age. It attacked people, and also mammoths and other big animals.

paragraphs.context: Jack was puzzled. The sorcerer had used both hands
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack cannot understand who is pulling the rope.
paragraphs.simple: Jack did not understand. The sorcerer used both his hands to help Annie, so someone else was holding the other end of the rope. Who was it?

paragraphs.context: Jack held on tight. He started up. His hands burned
paragraphs.mainIdea: Climbing up the rope is very hard for Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack held the rope hard and started to go up. His hands hurt. His arms hurt so much that he felt they might come out of his body.

paragraphs.context: The mammoth looked like a giant elephant
paragraphs.mainIdea: This tells us what the woolly mammoth looks like.
paragraphs.simple: The mammoth looked like a very big elephant. It had long, thick, red-brown hair and long teeth that turned up at the ends.

background.note: Woolly mammoths were about as big as African elephants today. They died out about 4,000 years ago. Scientists have found whole mammoths frozen in the ice in Siberia.

paragraphs.context: The great creature knelt down, just like a circus elephant
paragraphs.mainIdea: The mammoth gets down so the children can get on.
paragraphs.simple: The big animal went down on its knees, like an elephant in a circus show.

background.note: In the past, circuses often had trained elephants that did tricks. Many countries do not allow this now.

paragraphs.context: When the mammoth stood up, Jack gripped Annie’s coat
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is high up on the mammoth and holds on to Annie.
paragraphs.simple: When the mammoth stood up, Jack held Annie's coat hard so he would not fall. He felt very, very high above the ground.
paragraphs.tone: "Miles above the ground" is not true. It is a way to say "very high".

paragraphs.context: But at that moment the clouds parted, and the sun came out
paragraphs.mainIdea: The sun comes out, and the sorcerer disappears.
paragraphs.simple: The clouds moved apart and the sun came out. The light on the snow was so bright that Jack could not see. When he could see again, the sorcerer was gone.

paragraphs.context: They seemed to be escorting Jack and Annie back
paragraphs.mainIdea: The animals seem to walk with the children to keep them safe.
paragraphs.simple: The animals walked with them, like guards taking Jack and Annie home safely.

paragraphs.context: This is a great parade, Jack thought. Fantastic
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack loves riding with all the animals.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thought that walking with all these animals was like a wonderful parade.
paragraphs.tone: Jack feels happy and excited. The words in italics in the book are his thoughts, not words he says.

paragraphs.context: Behind them the sabertooth was slinking across the sunlit snow
paragraphs.mainIdea: The sabertooth is following them.
paragraphs.simple: The sabertooth was moving quietly behind them over the bright snow.

paragraphs.context: But Jack knew a sabertooth could kill any creature
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack knows the sabertooth can kill even a mammoth.
paragraphs.simple: Jack was afraid. He knew that a sabertooth could kill any animal, even a big mammoth.

paragraphs.context: Is she nuts? Jack thought
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack thinks Annie's idea is crazy.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thought Annie must be crazy to tell him to play music to a tiger.

paragraphs.context: The music sounded strange—as if it were coming from another world
paragraphs.mainIdea: The flute music sounds magical.
paragraphs.simple: The music was very strange. It did not sound like music from our world.

paragraphs.context: The mammoth walked away into the sunset
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lulu the mammoth goes away.
paragraphs.simple: The mammoth walked off toward the setting sun.
paragraphs.tone: This is where the book gets its name: "Sunset of the Sabertooth".

paragraphs.context: When Jack couldn’t see her anymore, he started up the lope ladder
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack climbs into the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: When Jack could not see the mammoth any more, he climbed up the rope ladder into the tree house.
paragraphs.tone: Note: "lope" is a printing mistake in this book. It should be "rope": "the rope ladder".

paragraphs.context: Jack smiled. Now he was positive they had found the third M thing
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is sure that the mammoth bone is the third M thing.
paragraphs.simple: Jack smiled. He was now sure that they had found the third thing that starts with M. Their job was done.
paragraphs.tone: The Pennsylvania book only comes back when the job is done, so now Jack knows the bone is the right thing.

paragraphs.context: The tallest person stepped forward and raised a spear
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Cro-Magnon man looks ready to throw a spear, so they leave.
paragraphs.simple: The tallest Cro-Magnon walked forward and held up a spear. Jack thinks it is time to go home.

paragraphs.context: He held up the mammoth bone. Then he placed it on the M
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack puts the mammoth bone next to the other two M things.
paragraphs.simple: Jack put the mammoth bone on the M on the floor, next to the mango and the moonstone.

paragraphs.context: Moonstone, mango, mammoth bone
paragraphs.mainIdea: They need one more M thing to free Morgan.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says the three things. They need just one more thing that starts with M. Then the magic on Morgan will end.

paragraphs.context: Their neighborhood looked rosy in the sunset
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is happy to be home in his own time.
paragraphs.simple: Their street looked pink in the evening sun. Jack thought it was good to be back in his own time, where it was warm and safe.

paragraphs.context: Yeah, Mom and Dad already did that
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie makes a joke about hunting at the supermarket.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says Mom and Dad already went "hunting" for dinner, at the supermarket.
paragraphs.tone: This is a joke. In the Ice Age people hunted animals for dinner. Today we just buy food at the supermarket.

paragraphs.context: I hope they trapped some spaghetti and meatballs
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack and Annie continue the hunting joke.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says he hopes his parents "caught" spaghetti and meatballs, and Annie hopes they "caught" a pizza.
paragraphs.tone: More of the joke: you can trap animals, but not spaghetti or pizza.

background.note: A favourite dinner in many American families: long noodles with small balls of meat in tomato sauce.

sentences.context: She traveled through time and space, gathering books for King Arthur’s library
sentences.simple: She went to different times and places, and she collected books for King Arthur's library.
sentences.main: She traveled through time and space.

parts.text: She traveled through time and space
parts.meaning: She went to other times and other places

parts.text: gathering books for King Arthur’s library
parts.job: What she did on her trips.
parts.meaning: and she collected books for King Arthur's library.

sentences.grammar: The "-ing" part after the comma tells you what she did while she traveled. "Time and space" means different times in history and different places in the world.

sentences.context: Now Jack and Annie and Peanut are about to set out in search of the third thing … in Sunset of the Sabertooth
sentences.simple: Now Jack, Annie and Peanut are going to start a trip very soon. They will look for the third special thing in this book, Sunset of the Sabertooth.
sentences.main: Jack and Annie and Peanut are about to set out.

parts.text: Now Jack and Annie and Peanut
parts.meaning: Now Jack, Annie and Peanut

parts.job: What they will do very soon.
parts.meaning: are going to start a trip very soon

parts.text: in search of the third thing
parts.meaning: to look for the third special thing

parts.job: Where you can read about it: the name of this book.
parts.meaning: in this book, Sunset of the Sabertooth.

sentences.grammar: "Be about to" means "be going to do it very soon". "Set out" means "start a trip". "In search of" means "looking for".

sentences.context: She and Jack were passing the Frog Creek woods on their way home from their swimming class at the Y
sentences.simple: Jack and Annie were walking past the woods. They were going home after their swimming class.
sentences.main: She and Jack were passing the woods.

parts.text: She and Jack were passing the Frog Creek woods
parts.meaning: Annie and Jack were walking past the Frog Creek woods
while they were going home

parts.text: from their swimming class at the Y
parts.meaning: from their swimming lesson at the YMCA sports centre.

sentences.grammar: "On their way home" means "while going home". Here "pass" means "go past", not "pass an exam". "The Y" is a short name for the YMCA.

sentences.context: On the M were a moonstone and a mango, the special things they’d found on their last two journeys
sentences.simple: A moonstone and a mango were on the M. They were the special things Jack and Annie found on their last two trips.
sentences.main: A moonstone and a mango were on the M.

parts.job: Where. This comes first, so the sentence is turned around.
parts.meaning: On the big letter M

parts.text: were a moonstone and a mango
parts.meaning: there were a moonstone and a mango

parts.text: the special things they’d found on their last two journeys
parts.job: More about them, after the comma.
parts.meaning: the special things they had found on their last two trips.

sentences.grammar: The place comes first, then the verb ("were"), then the things. In normal order: "A moonstone and a mango were on the M." "They'd found" means "they had found": they found them before this day.

sentences.context: During the late Ice Age in Europe, they sometimes lived in caves beneath cliffs
sentences.simple: Near the end of the Ice Age, some Cro-Magnons in Europe lived in caves under cliffs.
sentences.main: They sometimes lived in caves.

parts.text: During the late Ice Age in Europe
parts.meaning: Near the end of the Ice Age, in Europe,
the Cro-Magnons sometimes lived in caves
under tall rock walls.

sentences.grammar: The time comes first, before the comma. "Late Ice Age" means the last part of the Ice Age, not "too late". "Beneath" means "under".

sentences.context: Then they drove reindeer and mammoths into the traps
sentences.simple: Then they chased reindeer and mammoths, so the animals ran into the holes.
sentences.main: They drove animals into the traps.

parts.meaning: Then the hunters made
reindeer and mammoths
run into the holes.

sentences.grammar: Here "drove" does not mean driving a car. To "drive animals" means to chase them so they move where you want.

sentences.context: Most of your body heat is lost through your head
sentences.simple: Your body loses a lot of heat through your head.
sentences.main: Body heat is lost through your head.

parts.meaning: A lot of the warmth of your body
goes out
through your head.

sentences.grammar: "Is lost" tells you what happens to the heat, not what the heat does. Scientists today say we do not lose more heat through the head than through other parts, but covering your head still helps you stay warm.

sentences.context: These bears were larger and fiercer than today’s grizzlies
sentences.simple: These bears were bigger and more dangerous than the brown bears that live today.
sentences.main: These bears were larger than grizzlies.

parts.meaning: The cave bears were
bigger and more dangerous
than the grizzly bears that live now.

sentences.grammar: "-er ... than" compares two things. "Today's grizzlies" means the grizzly bears of today.

sentences.context: Their caves were filled with the bones of their ancestors
sentences.simple: Their caves were full of the bones of the bears that lived before them.
sentences.main: Their caves were filled with bones.

parts.meaning: The bears' caves were full

parts.text: with the bones of their ancestors
parts.meaning: of the bones of older bears from their families.

sentences.grammar: "Their" means the cave bears. "Filled with" means "full of". "Ancestors" are the family members who lived a long time before.

sentences.context: They made flute-like musical instruments from mammoth bones
sentences.simple: They made music pipes, like flutes, from the bones of mammoths.
sentences.main: They made instruments from bones.

parts.meaning: The Cro-Magnons made
things for playing music that were like flutes
from the bones of mammoths.

sentences.grammar: "Flute-like" means "like a flute". You can add "-like" to many nouns: "cat-like" eyes, "child-like" fun.

sentences.context: They used bone needles to sew the skins together for clothing
sentences.simple: They used needles made of bone to join the skins and make clothes.
sentences.main: They used bone needles.

parts.meaning: They used needles made from bone
to join the animal skins with thread
to make clothes.

sentences.grammar: "To + verb" after "used" tells you why. "Bone needles" means needles made of bone, like "stone lamps" means lamps made of stone.

sentences.context: They hollowed out a rock, filled it with animal fat, then burned a wick made from moss
sentences.simple: They made a hole in a rock and put animal fat in it. Then they lit a piece of moss in the fat, like a candle string.
sentences.main: They made a lamp in three steps.

parts.meaning: They made an empty space inside a rock,
put animal fat in it,

parts.text: then burned a wick made from moss
parts.meaning: and then lit a string made of moss.

sentences.grammar: This sentence lists three steps in order, with commas between them. "It" means the rock. "Made from moss" tells you about the wick.

sentences.context: Crouching clown, he hurried toward her
sentences.simple: He bent down low and hurried to her.
sentences.main: He hurried toward her.

parts.job: How he moved. (A printing mistake: read "Crouching down".)
parts.meaning: Bending down low,
he went quickly to Annie.

sentences.grammar: The "-ing" part at the start tells you how he moved. "Clown" is a mistake in this book; it should be "down".

sentences.context: They may have believed the paintings would give them power over the animals
sentences.simple: Maybe they thought the pictures could help them control the animals.
sentences.main: They may have believed something.

parts.job: What they maybe thought in the past.
parts.meaning: Maybe they thought

parts.text: the paintings would give them power over the animals
parts.meaning: that the pictures could help them control the animals and hunt well.

sentences.grammar: "May have + past form" means "maybe it was true in the past, but we are not sure". "Power over" something means you can control it.

sentences.context: He may have worn reindeer antlers so he could run like a reindeer—and an owl mask so he could see like an owl
sentences.simple: Maybe he wore reindeer horns to run fast like a reindeer, and an owl mask to see well like an owl.
sentences.main: He may have worn antlers and an owl mask.

parts.text: He may have worn reindeer antlers
parts.meaning: Maybe he wore reindeer horns

parts.text: so he could run like a reindeer
parts.meaning: so that he could run like a reindeer,
and maybe he wore an owl mask

parts.text: so he could see like an owl
parts.meaning: so that he could see like an owl.

sentences.grammar: "May have worn" means "maybe he wore; we are not sure". Each "so he could" gives a reason. The long line (—) adds the second thing.

sentences.context: The Cro-Magnons must have put branches over this hole
sentences.simple: The Cro-Magnons surely put branches over this hole.
sentences.main: They must have put branches over the hole.

parts.text: The Cro-Magnons must have put branches
parts.meaning: I am sure the Cro-Magnons put branches
on top of this hole.

sentences.grammar: "Must have + past form" means "I am almost sure this happened before". Jack did not see it, but he can guess.

sentences.context: The pit was too deep to climb out of
sentences.simple: The hole was so deep that they could not climb out.
sentences.main: The pit was too deep.

parts.meaning: The hole was very, very deep,
so they could not climb out.

sentences.grammar: "Too + adjective + to do" means "so ... that you cannot do it". The sentence ends with "of" because we say "climb out of the pit".

sentences.context: The sorcerer had used both hands to help Annie
sentences.simple: The sorcerer used both his hands to help Annie.
sentences.main: The sorcerer had used both hands.

parts.text: The sorcerer had used both hands
parts.meaning: The sorcerer used both his hands
to help Annie up.

sentences.grammar: "Had used" tells you it happened before Jack started to think about it. So who was holding the rope? The answer comes soon: the mammoth.

sentences.context: His arms felt as if they were being pulled out of their sockets
sentences.simple: His arms hurt so much that he felt they might come out of his shoulders.
sentences.main: His arms felt bad.

parts.meaning: His arms felt

parts.text: as if they were being pulled out of their sockets
parts.meaning: like someone was pulling them out of his shoulders.

sentences.grammar: "As if" means "like" and is used for something that is not really happening. His arms were not really coming out; it just felt that way.

sentences.context: The great creature knelt down, just like a circus elephant
sentences.simple: The big animal went down on its knees, like an elephant in a circus.
sentences.main: The great creature knelt down.

parts.meaning: The big animal went down on its knees,
in the same way as an elephant in a circus show.

sentences.grammar: "Creature" means any animal here. "Knelt" is the past of "kneel".

sentences.context: He nestled behind Annie, in the dip between the mammoth’s head and huge curved back
sentences.simple: He sat close behind Annie, in the low place between the mammoth's head and its big round back.
sentences.main: He nestled behind Annie.

parts.meaning: Jack sat close and comfortable behind Annie,
in the low place

parts.text: between the mammoth’s head and huge curved back
parts.meaning: between the mammoth's head and its big, round back.

sentences.grammar: Each part after the comma tells you more exactly where Jack sat. "Dip" here is a noun: a low place.

sentences.context: They seemed to be escorting Jack and Annie back to the tree house
sentences.simple: It looked like the animals were going with Jack and Annie to keep them safe on the way to the tree house.
sentences.main: They seemed to be escorting Jack and Annie.

parts.meaning: It looked like the animals were going with them to keep them safe,

parts.text: Jack and Annie back to the tree house
parts.meaning: taking Jack and Annie back to the tree house.

sentences.grammar: "Seemed to be ...ing" means "it looked like they were doing it". Jack is not sure; it only looks that way.

sentences.context: But Jack knew a sabertooth could kill any creature, including a mammoth
sentences.simple: But Jack knew that a sabertooth could kill any animal, even a mammoth.
sentences.main: Jack knew something bad.

parts.meaning: But Jack knew

parts.text: a sabertooth could kill any creature
parts.meaning: that a sabertooth could kill any animal,
even a mammoth.

sentences.grammar: "Including" means "and this one too". The word "that" is not written after "knew", but you can put it in: "Jack knew that ...".

sentences.context: The music sounded strange—as if it were coming from another world
sentences.simple: The music sounded strange, like it came from a different world.
sentences.main: The music sounded strange.

parts.meaning: The music was strange to hear

parts.text: —as if it were coming from another world
parts.meaning: like it was coming from a different world.

sentences.grammar: "As if it were" is used for something that is not really true. The music was not really from another world; it only sounded like it.

sentences.context: After they disappeared into the tree house, Jack climbed onto the ladder
sentences.simple: When Annie and Peanut were inside the tree house, Jack got onto the ladder.
sentences.main: Jack climbed onto the ladder.

parts.text: After they disappeared into the tree house
parts.meaning: When Annie and Peanut had gone into the tree house,
Jack got onto the ladder.

sentences.grammar: "After ..." at the start tells you what happened first. The main part comes after the comma.

sentences.context: It’s great to be back in this age, Jack thought
sentences.simple: Jack thought it was very good to be home in his own time.
sentences.main: Jack thought something.

parts.text: It’s great to be back in this age
parts.meaning: It is very good to be back in our own time,
Jack thought.

sentences.grammar: The words Jack thinks come first; "Jack thought" comes at the end. "This age" means our time today, the opposite of the Ice Age.
